summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. A 2024 Constitutional Court review of the surviving sodomy-law articles resolved that the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct; the articles that remained reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision covering heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy.

Enforcement against same-sex couples has historically run through public-order offences rather than a sodomy statute. A former law criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection, and a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code repealed it. In 2006 police closed several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo as part of a harassment programme. In 2012 officers intervened in the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag.

Visible political organising remains a trigger for official pressure. Reports indicate that openly visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility of changing their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35 and subsequently changed her name. The sources document no general legal route for changing a gender marker.

Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, a sectoral protection rather than a general one. In the Universal Periodic Review the country accepted recommendations on the rights of intersex persons and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; no domestic implementation detail is recorded for those commitments.

Family law statutes recognise no legal status between persons of the same sex, neither marriage nor civil or domestic partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55, under which the State shall promote and protect family organization based on marriage between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is barred at constitutional level. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on Private International Law could justify recognition of a foreign same-sex marriage, since a marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, the national law or the domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

Citizens have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programs for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organizations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Trans-specific care is not described in the sources.

Prevailing attitudes are restrictive. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, while only a plurality of 5% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway over public policy and surrounding attitudes, and the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation.
tangentialFactors:
Openly LGBTQ diplomatic visibility has produced organised backlash. The presentation of openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster with his husband in Santo Domingo in June 2015 was followed by attacks on LGBT Dominicans, evidence of organised domestic opposition, and sustained insult from religious leaders and some politicians. Evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." His departure in 2017 left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence, including speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016; his tenure exposed a polarised climate.

Organised trans advocacy exists and predates the current decade. COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, was co-founded in 2004; its executive director, Nairovi Castillo, has given first-hand accounts of trans struggles in the country. In April 2017 more than 300 activists from across the subregion attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo at which Dominican government officials spoke.

The absence of any anti-discrimination statute general enough to cover employment, housing or services places the Dominican Republic alongside regional jurisdictions where protections are confined to HIV-specific legislation, while its 2024 constitutional resolution on sodomy-law remnants places it among jurisdictions that have formally confirmed the non-criminalisation of same-sex conduct.
localsOnly:
Many LGBTQ Dominicans feel the need to remain in the closet, because discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity carries no legal consequence in employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services or public accommodations. The 2011 HIV/AIDS law supplies protection only in that narrow field.

Health services accessible to LGBTQ residents are largely HIV/AIDS education programs run by non-governmental organizations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos, rather than public trans-competent care. Routine public services carry no obligation to respect a person's gender identity.

The June 2018 executive decree enabled a legal name change for 35 named transgender Dominicans, including television journalist Mía Cepeda. It did not establish recognition of legal gender, and no repeatable administrative procedure for gender-marker change is documented.

Same-sex couples have no marital or partnership status in family law. They cannot register a relationship, and their households receive none of the rights attached to opposite-sex marriage, including in matters of inheritance, next-of-kin status and family registration.

Conservative Catholic and evangelical Protestant institutions carry significant weight in politics, and the major parties have not publicly backed LGBTQ rights legislation, which shapes the environment for openly visible community organising and for public displays of affection.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document entry or visa rules as they affect transgender visitors, gender-marker requirements on passports, or any screening at ports of entry that could result in a person being outed. Those points are unresolved from this inventory.

Whether Law 135/2011 is enforced in practice is not sourced. No record of penalties, complaints or remedies under the HIV/AIDS anti-discrimination provision appears here.

No hate-crime statute or protection machinery for bias-motivated violence against trans people is documented, and the inventory contains no incident data after the 2012 Pride Parade intervention.

Implementation of the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion remains unresolved in these sources, as does whether Article 41 of Law 544-14 has ever been applied to a foreign same-sex marriage by a Dominican court. Several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement the opinion; no implementing act is recorded.

Whether the June 2018 executive decree created a procedure open to other transgender Dominicans, or applied only to the 35 individuals named, is not sourced.

Trans-specific health care, and the availability of legal gender recognition on identity documents held by travellers, are not covered.
